item.title: The Minority Excuse: Measuring Rep. John Block Against His Own Caucus
item.description:
Twenty-five of 26 House Republicans had a bill signed into law in 2026. Block’s pass rate ranks 19th of 26, in the bottom 10 of his caucus. He led none of the bills that carry his name into law, and every proposal of his own failed.

ALAMOGORDO N.M. — When Rep. John Block’s thin legislative record comes up, the answer from his defenders is always the same. He is a Republican in a Democratic Legislature. The minority cannot pass bills. Judge him on something else.

So judge him against Republicans. We pulled the 2026 session record of every one of the 26 Republicans in the New Mexico House, the people who sit in the same minority, face the same committee chairs and answer to the same governor. Measured against them (fellow Republicans), Block is in the bottom third in effectiveness.

Block put his name on 37 bills, memorials and resolutions in 2026. Four passed but none that he actually sponsored to begin with. That is a success rate of 10.8%, and it ranks 19th in a caucus of 26. Only seven Republicans did worse. The caucus median is 13.8%. The average is 16.3%.

The members at the top are not household names with safe majorities behind them. Republican Rep. Jack Chatfield passed 42.9% of what he sponsored. Republicans; Rep. William Hall passed 33.3%. Rep. Brian Baca, 31.3%. Rep. Tanya Mirabal Moya, 27.3%. Rep. Catherine Cullen, a first-term member, 20.8%. Minority Leader Gail Armstrong passed seven of 40.

The bottom 10, in order, are Reps. Stefani Lord, Rebecca Dow, John Block, Alan Martinez, Jimmy Mason, Elaine Sena Cortez, Luis Terrazas, Rodney Montoya, Randall Pettigrew and Martin Zamora.

Cut the numbers another way and the picture holds. By the share of his measures that became law, Block is 18th. Among the 21 Republicans who sponsored at least 15 measures, he is 15th. Twenty-five of the 26 had a bill signed by the governor, so the minority can plainly pass legislation. First-term Republican Rep. Nicole Chavez had five.

A bill changes the law. A memorial is a statement of the Legislature’s wishes and changes nothing. A sponsor is anyone who signs on; the first-listed sponsor is the legislator who brought the bill and carried it.

Three bills that became law in 2026 have Block’s name on them. He was the first-listed sponsor on none. The medical malpractice overhaul was led by a Democrat, Rep. Christine Chandler, and by Armstrong; 49 legislators signed it, including 23 of the 26 House Republicans. The police battery bill was Rep. Andrea Reeb’s. The water project bill lists Democratic Rep. Kathleen Cates first and Block second, and came out of an interim committee. His one successful memorial, asking for a film industry task force, was a Democrat’s.

Everything Block brought on his own failed. Thirty-three measures, among them permitless carry of firearms, voter identification, chemical castration as a parole condition, a new tax on renewable energy production and year-round daylight saving time. Several were repeats of bills that failed in 2023. Most never got out of their first committee.

One of his measures passed the full House before dying in the Senate. Chavez had 13 reach that stage. Sena Cortez had nine. Armstrong, Cullen and Rep. Jenifer Jones had eight each. Those are bills that Democratic chairs agreed to hear and Democratic members agreed to vote for. That takes relationships.

Block’s campaign postcard tells voters he “delivered more than $11 million for Alamogordo and Otero County priorities.”

Here is how that money works. Each year the House divides its share of capital outlay evenly. Each member turns in a list of projects, the lists are folded into one bill, and the bill passes or fails as a package. A legislative finance handout put the 2025 share at $2.5 million for every representative. The Legislative Council Service chart for 2026 shows seven projects under Block’s name totaling exactly $2.5 million, the same figure it shows for Armstrong and Baca. The money on the postcard is the standard share, added up over four years.

Then look at how he voted on the packages. In 2023 he voted no on House Bill 505. In 2025 he voted no on House Bill 450, and no on the state budget. In 2026 he voted no on Senate Bill 240 and no on the capital outlay reauthorization bill. He picked the projects, voted against the bills that paid for them, and mailed voters a card taking credit.

In the final week of the 2026 session he was also recorded absent on four bills, including wheelchair insurance coverage and the Child Care Assistance Program Act.

Block came to Santa Fe as the publisher of the Piñon Post, a site that, as the Santa Fe New Mexican has reported, routinely labels Democrats “far-left.” Before he held office he filed a campaign finance complaint against the governor over hair and makeup expenses; the Secretary of State’s Office found no violation. In November 2024 the secretary of state told a legislative committee she had been harassed online, and her office named Block as the member she meant. Block denied it and called the accusation a publicity stunt.

No record can prove that those fights are why his bills die. That is a conclusion after speaking with members of both parties that work along side him. 

But the contrast in the data is hard to miss. The Republicans who passed bills in 2026 attached themselves to work that could win Democratic votes: licensing compacts to bring health care workers into the state, parole and pension fixes, property tax relief for disabled veterans. 

Block spent his session on bills with no path, in a building where the people he has spent years attacking decide what gets a hearing.

Four years in, his record is 174 measures sponsored and 11 signed bills carrying his name. Being in the minority explains why Republican bills are hard to pass. It does not explain why 18 other Republicans passed a larger share of theirs.

District 51 voters have a choice this year, that by Block's Party's own admission has become "a race of a lifetime." Unlike Block, Grace Nagamine is  a lifelong Alamogordo resident running as an independent, and claims to be beholden to the constituents not the party ideology of either party and  is on the Nov. 3 ballot against Block.

Where Block offers a mailer, Nagamine has published detailed position statements and draft legislation at graceforhd51.org, so voters can read what she would file before they vote. Where Block has built a brand on picking fights with the people who run the Capitol, she has committed to building collaborations with members of both parties. As an independent she owes neither caucus a vote.

The case for that approach is in the numbers above. Collaboration is how dollars and support reach rural New Mexico communities. The capital outlay packages, the water project authorizations and the licensing compacts all moved because legislators of both parties put their names on the same bill and then voted for it. Alamogordo has $160 million in water and sewer repairs ahead of it and will need every state dollar it can get.

One candidate has spent four years showing how he does the job, the numbers say ineffectively. The other is telling voters, in writing, how she would do it differently. Early voting begins Oct. 6.

item.title: Letter on City Hall Workplace Concerns Reaches Commission, Press and Former City Leaders; City Manager Responds
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — An anonymous letter raising workplace conduct concerns at Alamogordo City Hall has reached the mayor and City Commission, city administration, AlamogordoTownNews and former members of the city’s staff leadership.

The letter repeats concerns that city employees first described to AlamogordoTownNews for our Oct. 1 commentary. City Manager Robert Stockwell confirmed Monday that City Hall received it, and he responded in writing the same evening.

The letter’s author is unknown and its claims have not been verified. AlamogordoTownNews is withholding the names, titles and departments it identifies, along with details that could point to specific employees, given allegations are not proven. 

Who received the letter

The letter is addressed to the mayor, the mayor pro tem, the five city commissioners and Human Resources. Stockwell confirmed City Hall received it Monday and said it “has been distributed to the Mayor and Commissioners.”

AlamogordoTownNews received the same letter by mail, in an envelope postmarked Oct. 3. Copies also went to former members of the city’s staff leadership, AlamogordoTownNews has learned.

That distribution puts the concerns in front of people inside and outside current city government. The writer identifies as a city employee. “I am making this report anonymously because I am afraid of retaliation,” the letter states.

What the letter raises

The one-page letter raises three concerns and asks that each be looked into.

• Perceived favoritism. The writer describes what appears to be a close relationship between senior leaders, including long closed-door meetings. Employees believe it gives one department head outsized access and influence, the letter says, and it is hurting morale. The writer states they have not personally witnessed anything physical or romantic and do not want to claim otherwise.

 A possible conflict of interest. The writer asks whether a relationship between two senior staff members of equal rank could lead to different treatment in city financial decisions. The writer says they were told the relationship does not violate city policy.

Comments about an employee’s appearance. The writer reports, under the city’s sexual harassment policy, hearing a supervisor comment more than once on a subordinate’s physical appearance. The comments were not directed at the  letter writer.

The writer says the report is not meant to cause trouble. The letter cites the city’s stated zero-tolerance policy and asks that the concerns “at least be looked into.”

The city manager responds

Stockwell answered in three emails to AlamogordoTownNews on Monday evening.

He denied any improper conduct on his own part.

“There is no improper relationship between me and any employees of the city,” he wrote. He said he fully understands his role and would not compromise his impartiality and professionalism toward city employees, or the integrity of any employee.

He said private meetings with senior staff are routine.

“I routinely meet with the senior staff behind closed doors dealing with matters that must be kept confidential and/or often to simply block out conversations and noise from hallways and adjoining offices.”

On the harassment report, he gave a one-sentence commitment: “The allegation of sexual harassment will be handled in full accordance with City policy.”

On the conflict-of-interest question, Stockwell pointed to oversight. “The city’s finances are ultimately the responsibility of the city manager who is accountable to the city commission,” he wrote. Anyone suggesting favored treatment toward a department, he added, “simply doesn’t understand the checks and balances built into the systems.”

He also wrote that relationships between colleagues “are neither inappropriate nor unusual in our society.” Six minutes later he sent a clarification: “What I meant to say was ‘co-equal colleagues.’”

The emails did not say who will conduct the harassment review, whether it will be handled inside City Hall or by an outside party, or when it will conclude.

How it ties to our earlier reporting

The Oct. 1 commentary drew on accounts from several city employees over the prior 60 days. They described comments about a coworker’s appearance, a perception that favor shapes how staff are treated, and fear of speaking up.

The letter covers the same ground. It describes a remark about an employee’s appearance that closely resembles one those employees recounted, and the writer says they heard it firsthand. It also describes the same perception of preferential treatment for staff seen as close to top administration.

The letter is not independent proof. It was postmarked two days after the commentary ran, and AlamogordoTownNews cannot determine whether its author is among the employees who spoke to us earlier.

What has changed is the record.

The concerns are now in writing before the commission and Human Resources, they have circulated beyond City Hall, and the city manager has answered them on the record.

What comes next

The mayor and commissioners now have the letter, and the city manager has committed to handling the harassment report under city policy. The next regular City Commission meeting is Tuesday, Oct. 13, at 6:30 p.m.

Our Oct. 1 commentary called for an independent review of workplace complaints by an outside firm or attorney reporting to the full commission. Whether the commission will take that step is not yet known. The public should demand it and the commission should insist on it and a public report should be made on how to get the city’s house in order which now appears to be running amok. 

The writer’s fear of retaliation is addressed in law. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act makes it illegal to retaliate against an employee who reports harassment or cooperates with an investigation.

This is a developing story.

AlamogordoTownNews will report on any review, its outcome and rather the majority of the commission members act in a manner of professionalism and transparency. The commission should require the city manager to hire an experienced and external legal review of the complaints, policies and recent cultural that had led to these allegations. Stay tuned.

item.title: Soccer and Football Area Results
item.description:
Alamogordo shut out Deming 2-0, scoring twice before halftime and getting a penalty-kick save from goalkeeper Noah Mirabal to protect the lead.

Levi Ramirez and Max Cadoret each found the net for the Tigers, and Kyle Tamayo assisted on both goals. Cadoret's goal came in the 31st minute and sent Alamogordo into the break up 2-0.

Deming's best chance to get back into the match came in the 61st minute on a penalty kick, but Mirabal turned it away. He finished with seven saves in the shutout.

The win moves the Tigers to 5-9-2. They play next at Centennial on Thursday.

item.title: First-Time Candidates Find Common Ground at Alamogordo Forum
item.description:
LAMOGORDO — Democrats, Republicans and Independents shared a stage at Otero Arts on Tuesday night, and the conversation stayed civil from start to finish.

Alamogordo Town News and KALHRadio.org hosted the nonpartisan candidate forum Oct. 6 as part of their monthly Voices of Alamogordo series. Three candidates for county commission took part, along with candidates for the state Legislature.

The forum came four weeks before the Nov. 3 general election. It gave voters a chance to question the candidates face to face.

Every candidate on stage was running for office for the first time. That put a slate of new faces in front of voters and added a new dimension to this year's election.

Each candidate opened with a statement explaining why they are running. Each then laid out their top priorities for the office they are seeking.

Questions followed from two directions. Audience members submitted a selection, and moderator Chris Edwards added his own. Across party lines, the candidates showed deep passion for their convictions.

Editor's note: add each candidate's name, party and the seat sought.

The Republican candidate told the audience he had been advised not to attend. He came anyway, and said the reception was warm and not what he had been warned to expect.

His remark fit the evening. One line of questioning asked the candidates how residents can get along and bridge the political divide, in the region and across the country. The discussion that followed was civil and positive, and the dialogue stayed warm and friendly throughout.

Organizers had asked for exactly that. The forum announcement said civility and decorum are the standard at Voices of Alamogordo events, for candidates and audience members alike.

Policy questions covered four main areas, among others.

The result was an informative discussion that let voters hear the candidates side by side.

About 47 people attended in person at Otero Arts, 1118 Indiana Ave. The livestream had drawn about 120 views by Wednesday.

The forum is one of many meet-the-candidate events planned across the region this month. Voices of Alamogordo forums are held on the first Tuesday of each month.

The full forum is available on KALH Radio's YouTube channel.

item.title: News and Analysis: Block Sponsored a 2026 Tax Increase on PNM's & Other Utilities Power. State Analysts Said Ratepayers Would Pay
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. —News and Analysis:  Kelly and James Metcalf raise five children on one income. On Sept. 17 they opened a PNM bill for $1,949.26. The same stretch last year cost about $506. Johnny Martin, 74, spent $12,000 on a new air conditioner and appliances and still got four straight bills over $400. 

Residents packed a town hall to tell regulators their bills had doubled or tripled. Regulators blame a meter-reader shortage and a two-stage rate increase.

Rep. John Block was in the room, and regulators praised him for coming. One of his neighbors did not. Tanya Burns told the crowd that Block is seldom around, that he has not responded to her on a number of issues, and that he has not been an advocate for affordable power. She called his appearance political theater weeks before an election. 

Those are her views. The record below is why its important to review rather or not that she has a point.

The bill

Block sponsored House Bill 113 in 2026. It would have taxed electricity generated from renewable resources at 3.75% of its wholesale value, starting Jan. 1, 2027.  A similar bill was filed in 2025. 

In 2025, 57% of PNM's generation came from wind and solar. 

What it would have cost

The Taxation and Revenue Department projected the tax would collect $27.45 million in its first half-year and between $56.5 million and $59.8 million in each of the next three years.  That is more than $200 million collected from renewable generators statewide in three and a half years.

The state's energy department said the tax would increase retail electricity prices for New Mexico ratepayers, that is those very locals already complaining about their PNM Bill last week to the PRC. It was estimated at roughly $3 per megawatt-hour in added cost during peak months of 2024. 

That did not cause the Metcalfs' bill to increase because Block's bill got no where. It was a charge in the wrong direction, every month, while bills are already climbing, sponsored by Block who claims he is there for you the concerned consumer.

The damage beyond the bill

The monthly charge is the smallest part of what the state's analysts warned about.

None of the money would have come back to ratepayers. It was directed to the Severance Tax Permanent Fund.

If the goal was fairness, why raise a tax?

The rate in Block's bill, 3.75%, matches the state's severance tax rate on oil and gas. One state analysis described the bill as taxing renewable energy in a way similar to that tax.  The apparent argument is parity: if oil and gas pay, wind and solar should too.

There are two ways to make two tax rates equal. You can raise the lower one or cut the higher one. Block chose to raise one.

That is a notable choice for this legislator who claims to be a fiscal conservative.  On energy, he filed a tax increase, and it landed on the power source that supplies most of this city's electricity.

This outlet's editorial stance is limited government. A new excise tax, stacked on an existing one, with a $3.5 million bureaucracy to collect it, is not that.

In 2024 Block voted against raising royalty rates on new oil and gas wells on state land. In 2026 he co-sponsored a bill, as its third sponsor, to have combined-cycle natural gas counted as renewable.  So he has opposed higher charges on oil and gas, backed a friendlier label for gas, and proposed a new tax on wind and solar.

None of his 2026 energy bills advanced.  Voters should still ask why the tax was filed twice?

It's been reported in Santa Fe that he is in a race for his life. Per Tanya Burns comments and the analysis that followed it is clearly, why!

Grace Nagamine, the independent on the Nov. 3 ballot, has her specific position on PNM billing and utility costs, are found in videos one her campaign Facebook Page.

Block has declined to speak with Alamogordo Town News, was invited to an upcoming community forum and has not responded.  Written questions about this article, including why he chose a new tax instead of a cut, were sent on 10/5/26 and were not answered by publication. 

ATN will publish his response in full if he provides one.

item.title: Joseph Vazquez Arrested for First Degree Child Abuse
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A 22-year-old Alamogordo man has been arrested and charged with first-degree child abuse after a 1-year-old boy was taken to a hospital with injuries police described as suspicious.

Officers with the Alamogordo Police Department were called to Christus Health Southern New Mexico on Sept. 26 in reference to the child's injuries, the department said in a news release Tuesday. The boy was transported to University Medical Center because of his injuries.

Police said their investigation identified Joseph Vazquez as the suspect. He is charged with abuse of a child resulting in great bodily harm, a first-degree felony, and was booked into the Otero County Detention Center pending a court appearance.

The department did not release details about the child's condition, the nature of the injuries, or Vazquez's relationship to the child.

Police are asking anyone with additional information to come forward. Detectives can be reached at 575-439-4300.

A criminal charge is an accusation. Vazquez is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

item.title: Early voting has begun in Otero County - Alamogordo
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Voters turned out briskly as in-person voting for the 2026 general election opened in Otero County on Tuesday, with early reports showing several hundred ballots already cast in Alamogordo.

The opening-day traffic came through the County Clerk’s sub-office in the County Administration Building, 1101 New York Ave., Room 101. It is the county’s only in-person voting site until expanded early voting begins Oct. 17.

By the close of business, several ballots had been cast, according to.

Candidates spent Tuesday night pushing for exactly that kind of start. At a community forum, Liam Griffin, candidate for NM Senate and Grace Nagamine, an independent running for state House District 51, were among those who urged supporters to get to the polls during early voting rather than wait for Election Day.

Tuesday was also the day the clerk’s office began mailing absentee ballots, and the last day to register to vote by mail or online. Residents who missed that deadline can still register or update their registration in person at any early voting location through Election Day, Nov. 3.

The ballot is topped by races for governor and U.S. Senate, along with congressional, legislative and local offices.

Voting options widen later this month, with early voting sites opening in Alamogordo, Mescalero and Chaparral and one-day mobile stops in Tularosa and Cloudcroft.

Where to vote

In-person absentee voting continues at the County Clerk’s sub-office in the County Administration Building, 1101 New York Ave., Room 101, in Alamogordo. Hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday through Oct. 30, and 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 31.

Early voting at the Otero County Fairgrounds, 401 Fairgrounds Road in Alamogordo, runs Oct. 17 through Oct. 31. Hours are 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday.

Mobile voting comes to the Tularosa Public Safety Facility, 609 St. Francis Drive, on Saturday, Oct. 17, and to Cloudcroft High School, 10 Swallow Place, on Saturday, Oct. 24. Both run from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

In Mescalero, early voting is offered at the Inn of the Mountain Gods, 287 Carrizo Canyon Road, from Wednesday, Oct. 28, through Friday, Oct. 30. Hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

In Chaparral, the Far South Fire Station, 827 Luna St., is open Thursday, Oct. 29, through Saturday, Oct. 31, from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Key dates

The last day to request an absentee ballot is Oct. 20. Early and in-person absentee voting end Oct. 31. Election Day is Nov. 3.

Voters can check their registration or apply for an absentee ballot at NMVote.org.

item.title: Lincoln County Tells Requester to Ask Its Private Jail Contractor for Records on In-Custody Death, Then Calls Request “Closed”
item.description:
CARRIZOZO — More than two months after a person died in custody at the Lincoln County Detention Center, the public still has no staffing records, no surveillance video, no jail contract, and no medical-staff communications from the county that is legally responsible for the facility.

What Lincoln County has offered instead, in an Oct. 6 letter from the Sheriff’s Office, is a single redacted incident report and 115 photographs, available on paper for $74.50. For nearly everything else, the letter gives the same answer five times: go ask the private company that runs the jail yourself. The County did not forward the request to the contractor or retrieve the records from it. It then declares the request “closed.”

Alamogordo Town News, which filed the request, has formally objected. In a letter sent Oct. 6, ATN told the County that the response violates the Inspection of Public Records Act in several respects and gave it until Oct. 16 to fix them before ATN seeks enforcement in district court.

The stakes have since risen. On Sept. 28, a second inmate died in the jail’s custody, and ATN has a second records request pending.

Disclosure: The author of this article is the requester and a party to this dispute as a part of our efforts at journalism to keep the public in the loop via records requests and transparency. 

What ATN asked for

The death occurred on the night of July 29 or the early morning of July 30. ATN has reported it as a suicide, based on sources inside the jail and the judiciary; no official finding has been released. 

On July 31, ATN asked Lincoln County for five categories of records: the investigation file; three years of jail staffing, overtime, and turnover data; surveillance video from the hours around the death; the county’s jail operating contract and renewal file; and communications from jail healthcare staff raising safety concerns in the preceding 90 days.

The request was aimed at questions the incident report alone cannot answer: how many officers were on duty that night, how long they had been working, whether anyone had warned administrators about staffing or suicide-prevention gaps, and what the county’s contract requires of its operator.

The response

The County acknowledged the request the day it arrived. On Aug. 17, the last day allowed, it invoked the law’s “excessively burdensome or broad” provision and gave itself until Sept. 18. ATN answered the next day, clarifying dates and asking that simple items, such as the contract itself, be released without waiting.

In September, the County answered through its attorney. It said it was withholding the incident reports, the medical examiner’s report, the video, and the healthcare communications because of an ongoing investigation. It said staffing rosters, safety inspections, and cell-visibility records were held by the jail’s private operator. And it said its next update would come in mid-December. ATN sent a written demand on Sept. 29 seeking faster release.

The Oct. 6 letter, signed by Sheriff’s Office Records Coordinator Sam E. Chavez, states that the office “received” the request on Sept. 28, which is 59 days after the County did, and demonstrates another violation of IPRA by the county. It addresses only the first category. For staffing, video, contract, and healthcare records, it tells ATN to request them from Correctional Solutions Group, LLC, the private operator of the detention center.

The letter also withholds 45 photographs, stating only that they cannot be released “due to graphic nature of photo.” It describes the incident report as “redacted” without saying what was removed or why. And it asserts that all Sheriff’s Office records exist in paper format, billing 149 pages at 50 cents each. IPRA does not distinguish and exception for graphic photos. 

Two answers from one county

The Sheriff’s letter does not match what the County’s attorney told ATN days earlier. The County said incident reports were being withheld because of an ongoing investigation; the Sheriff’s Office is now offering its incident report for sale. The County said its next update would come in mid-December; the Sheriff’s Office says the request is closed. Neither letter explains the other.

A second death

On Monday, Sept. 28 — the same day the Sheriff’s Office says it received the July request — a 24-year-old inmate died at the detention center. The inmate, who has not been identified, was reportedly being held on behalf of the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs.

Accounts of the death conflict. ATN and KALH Radio first reported it as an apparent suicide, based on sources within the jail and the judiciary. A jail staff member has since told ATN that the inmate was diabetic, was going through alcohol withdrawal, and died in a cell equipped with a camera.

A family member of the deceased has now confirmed that he was released from the hospital to the jail. The family is unsure if any medical staff was available at the jail as they are getting a run around from jail officials they have stated and not getting answers. An attorney is going be hired by the family they said. His name is being withheld out of respect for the family as they settle his affairs.

 That staff member, who is employed through the jail and spoke on condition of anonymity citing fear of retaliation, also said the jail currently has no medical provider issuing orders, did not that day when the death occured — the kind of orders that would govern blood glucose checks and insulin for a diabetic inmate.

None of that has been officially confirmed by the IPRA request. The Office of the Medical Investigator has not released a cause of death. The warden declined to discuss the death in an interview with KALH Radio, saying such cases go to the Sheriff’s Office, and said healthcare at the jail is provided through WSI, a Colorado company. WSI describes itself as a staffing firm. ATN has asked the County, the warden, Correctional Solutions Group, WSI, and the Sheriff’s Office who currently issues medical orders at the jail. WSI has placed a gag order on its staff per sources within the jail.

ATN filed a second IPRA request on seeking records on the September death. It is pending.

The second death sharpens the questions behind the first request. Healthcare staff communications raising safety concerns and jail staffing levels are among the records the County has withheld or told ATN to get from the contractor. Both bear directly on whether an inmate with a chronic condition could be monitored and treated.

Correctional Solutions Group, of Tyler, Texas, is paid about $5.45 million a year to run the jail. Its contract expires Jan. 27, 2027, and county commissioners will soon decide whether to renew it.

Why ATN says that is not lawful

IPRA defines public records as those held “by or on behalf of” a public body. New Mexico appellate courts have applied that language to private contractors performing government functions, including a private medical provider in the state’s jails and prisons. 

ATN’s position is that a county can hire a company to run its jail but cannot hire away its duty to produce the records. A private company has no records custodian under IPRA and no statutory deadline.

The instruction is hardest to explain for the contract. Lincoln County is a party to its own jail agreement and holds a copy. When a request lands with the wrong office, the law requires the custodian to forward it to the right one and tell the requester, not to send the requester to a vendor.

ATN’s letter also objects that “graphic nature” is not an exception found in IPRA, that a denial must cite its legal basis and name the officials responsible, that redactions require explanation, and that records requested electronically must be provided that way when they exist electronically. An incident report with a system-generated case number and 115 photographs were, in all likelihood, not created on paper.

What the County may have right

Not every withholding is a violation. State law does contain an exception for certain law enforcement images. The County has not cited that provision or said which photographs it covers. Likewise, 50 cents a page is within the $1 cap the law sets for paper copies. ATN’s objection is to being charged for printouts of digital files it asked to receive by email, and to release being conditioned on payment when inspection in person is free.

The inmate’s own medical and mental health records are also likely to be confidential under other law. ATN’s complaint is that the County has not tied any withholding to a specific exception. Its attorney cited an “ongoing investigation,” but the New Mexico Supreme Court held in 2020 that an ongoing investigation does not by itself justify withholding an entire file.

The video clock

Jail surveillance systems typically record over old footage on a fixed schedule. ATN asked the County on Sept. 29, and again on Oct. 6, to confirm in writing that it has instructed Correctional Solutions Group to preserve video and related records. The Sheriff’s Oct. 6 letter does not address preservation. The same question now applies to the camera-equipped cell where the second inmate died. 

A regional pattern

Lincoln County is not the first southern New Mexico government ATN has had to press on records. ATN is currently in district court against the Alamogordo City Commission over open-meetings and records claims, and has a separate enforcement dispute with the Timberon Water and Sanitation District which will likely end in litigation. 

The details differ. The pattern is familiar: long delay, partial answers, and a requester left to decide whether to sue.

IPRA anticipates that. A public body that fails to respond properly to a written request can face damages of up to $100 a day, and a requester who prevails in court is entitled to costs. Those bills are paid by taxpayers.

ATN will provide an updates as soon as records are produced or litigation for such records is filed. Stay tuned...

item.title: His Poorest Constituents Needed Relief on Power Bills. Block Voted No, Twice.
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Twice in 2025, Rep. John Block had the chance to back a path to lower electric bills for the poorest households in his own district. Twice he voted no.

This summer those households opened PNM bills that had doubled and tripled. One topped $1,900. A 73-year-old lifelong resident watched his climb from $70 to $172.

House Bill 91 was written for people like them, in a county where nearly one in five residents lives in poverty and nearly one in five is 65 or older. Block, R-Alamogordo, was the only member of his committee to oppose it, and he voted against it again on the House floor. It became law over his objection.

The vote

House Bill 91, the Public Utility Rate Structures Act, passed the New Mexico House 42-25 on Feb. 25, 2025. Block voted no, according to the official House roll call.

It was his second no in what should be consumer friendly protections on utilities or PNM bills. On Feb. 7, 2025, the House Government, Elections and Indian Affairs Committee sent the bill forward 8-1. The committee report records Block as the lone vote against.

The bill does not set a rate. It lets investor-owned utilities, including PNM, design a lower rate or an assistance program for low-income customers and take it to the Public Regulation Commission, which must approve it before it takes effect.

On the House floor, Block argued it was not just for one customer to pay a different rate than another based only on income, according to NM Political Report's account of the debate. Other Republicans said the discount would shift costs onto middle-income households that are also struggling.

The Senate passed the bill 26-16 on March 20, 2025. The governor signed it on April 11, 2025.

Who is exposed

Nearly one in five Otero County residents lives below the poverty line, and nearly one in five is 65 or older. Those are the households a low-income rate is built for, and the ones with the least room to absorb a doubled bill.

About 12,600 county residents, or 19.3%, live below the poverty line, according to Census Bureau survey data. About 12,800, or 18.3%, are 65 or older.

Among those seniors, 12.9% live below the poverty line. In 12.7% of the county's households, a person 65 or older lives alone. The median household income is $55,876.

The county's poverty rate is nearly double the national rate of 10.6% in the same Census table. Its median household income runs about two-thirds of the national figure.

These are county numbers. District 51 covers a large part of Otero County, centered on Alamogordo, but not all of it, and the Census does not publish this profile by House district.

The scale of the billing problem is also on record. PNM told the PRC that 8,764 meters are in the affected area, many of them put on estimated or delayed billing after July 21, Alamogordo Town News reported.

The bills

The spike has a documented cause, and it is not a vote. PNM told regulators in July that it was short of meter readers in Alamogordo and Ruidoso, according to the PRC. The shortage produced more estimated bills and, for some customers, delayed ones.

At the PRC's Sept. 29 town hall at the Sgt. Willie Estrada Memorial Civic Center, residents brought bills that had doubled or tripled. One topped $1,900, NM Political Report reported. A 73-year-old lifelong resident said his bill went from $70 to $172.

Several residents said PNM billed two months on one statement, which pushed their usage into the highest-priced tier. PRC staff also pointed to a two-stage rate increase that took effect in summer 2025 and April 2026, and conceded it was not well communicated, according to Alamogordo Town News. A record heat wave in early August added to usage, the Albuquerque Journal reported.

PNM has suspended disconnections and late fees for affected customers, is offering payment arrangements, and has promised true-up bills once actual readings are in. Corrections may keep landing on statements through October, the PRC told KRQE. The PRC docket is case 26-0000147.

None of that traces to House Bill 91. Block's vote did not cause a meter-reader shortage, a heat wave or a rate case.

What the vote shows is where he stood: when the Legislature created a path to lower bills for the poorest customers, the representative for Alamogordo voted against the interests of his own constituents, twice.

The two arguments

Grace Nagamine, the independent challenging Block on Nov. 3, has campaigned on the bills since August. That month she published step-by-step instructions for filing complaints with the PRC and the attorney general.

Her case against Block on this vote is narrow. The Legislature offered a tool aimed at low-income households. He opposed it in committee and on the floor. The households it was written for are the ones now holding the largest bills relative to income.

Block's case is the one he made in 2025. A discount for one group is paid for by everyone else on the system, and a household just above the income cutoff can be struggling too. Opponents of the bill, including the group Better Together New Mexico, told lawmakers that fixed-income customers who do not qualify would end up subsidizing those who do.

Block attended the Sept. 29 town hall. One resident who spoke called his presence political theater with the election weeks away, Alamogordo Town News reported.

Early voting began Oct. 6. True-up bills are expected to keep arriving through the month. Do we want a state representative that does not vote to lower the bills for his constituents? Isn’t it time to expel the incumbents? Are you better off now than you were 2 years ago economically? If not vote out the incumbents.

item.title: Alamogordo golf sweeps Ruidoso, lands both teams in top three at Rio Rancho
item.description:
Alamogordo's golf teams made the most of a busy two days, sweeping the team and individual titles at Monday's Ruidoso Fall Classic before posting top-three finishes at Tuesday's Rio Rancho Shootout.

At Twin Warriors Golf Club on Tuesday, the Alamogordo boys shot 309 to finish second, five strokes behind champion Los Alamos and four ahead of La Cueva.

Brody Wright and Dyson Wright each carded a 72 to tie for second individually. For Brody Wright, that was a seven-stroke improvement on his round a day earlier. Landon Wright placed ninth with a 77, Kolton Stagner tied for 12th at 79, Andrez Montoya tied for 19th at 81 and Jacobi Saldevar tied for 42nd at 89.

The Alamogordo girls took third with a 354, six strokes back of runner-up Organ Mountain. Ellie Clore led the Tigers with an 82 to tie for 10th. Ava Armijo was 14th at 87, Kylee Wright 18th at 92, Annelisia Herrera tied for 19th at 93 and Charli Ramsey tied for 22nd at 95.

A day earlier at The Links at Sierra Blanca, Alamogordo left little doubt. Dyson Wright fired a 70 to win the boys individual title and lead the Tigers to a team score of 295. Landon Wright was third with a 73, Stagner fourth at 75 and Montoya sixth at 77. Brody Wright tied for seventh at 79 and Saldevar was 12th at 82, putting all six Alamogordo golfers in the top 12.

Armijo claimed the girls individual crown with a 77 as Alamogordo won with a 337. Clore finished fourth at 86, Herrera and Ramsey tied for fifth at 87, and Kylee Wright tied for eighth at 90.

Both teams return to action Oct. 19 at the Buddy Carazzi Invite at Riverside Country Club in Carlsbad.

item.title: Tularosa outlasts Capitan in five-set thriller and other Volleyball action
item.description:
Tularosa survived a marathon fifth set to beat Capitan 3-2 on Tuesday night, the lone win for Otero County volleyball teams on a night when Alamogordo and Cloudcroft were both swept.

The Lady Cats won 21-25, 25-20, 11-25, 25-23, 20-18, twice rallying from a set down. Capitan took the third set by 14 points and stood one set from the match. Tularosa edged the fourth by two, then outlasted Capitan in a deciding set that ran five points past the usual 15.

Capitan outscored Tularosa 111-102 across the five sets and still lost. The win moves the Lady Cats to 4-10.

Alamogordo opened district play with a straight-set loss to Centennial, 25-9, 25-13, 25-14. The Lady Tigers did not reach 15 points in any set and fell to 6-9 overall, 0-1 in district.

Cloudcroft lost to Hot Springs 25-8, 25-14, 25-18. The Lady Bears scored more points in each successive set but could not extend the match, and their record slipped to 8-5.

item.title: Otero County family tie reported in deadly Lea County pipeline explosion
item.description:
Two people died Tuesday near Eunice; officials have not released names or a cause

An Otero County mother said in a social media post that her son was one of the two people killed Tuesday in a pipeline explosion in the Lea County oilfield.

The claim has not been verified. Out of sensitivity to the family, this publication is not reporting her son's name or other unconfirmed details until official sources verify them.

Authorities have not publicly identified either victim. The Lea County Sheriff's Office said the names are being withheld pending notification of next of kin, and that no further details will be released while the investigation is active.

Deputies were called at about 1:04 p.m. Tuesday, Oct. 6, to an industrial accident involving a fire on a pipeline in the oilfield near Highway 176 and Bootleg Road, west of Eunice, the sheriff's office said. Two people were found dead at the scene.

Lea County officials placed the explosion near Paduca Breaks and Alisha Lane. The Eunice and Jal fire departments, the sheriff's office and the county Office of Emergency Management responded.

No evacuations were ordered and no structures were damaged, the county said. Lease roads in the area were closed temporarily while company representatives worked with emergency crews.

The sheriff's office called it an isolated incident and said there is no ongoing threat to the public.

Officials have not said what caused the explosion, what work was under way at the time, or which company owns or operates the line. They also have not said who employed the two people who died.

The Lea County explosion was one of two pipeline emergencies in New Mexico on Tuesday. A ruptured gas line near La Boca in San Juan County sent flames about 100 feet into the air and started a wildfire, according to the Santa Fe New Mexican.

This story will be updated as more information is released.

item.title: Corks & Shells returns to Alameda Park with a bigger pour list, Oct 17, 2026
item.description:

item.title: Sierra Club backs independent Grace Nagamine in Otero County House District 51 Race
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Sierra Club's Rio Grande Chapter has endorsed independent Grace Nagamine for New Mexico House District 51. The move puts the environmental group behind the challenger to Rep. John Block in a district covering much of Otero County.

The chapter announced the endorsement on Facebook this week. Nagamine also appears on its 2026 general election slate, which covers contested statewide, legislative and local races and ballot questions.

The chapter's Political Committee said Nagamine impressed members with her knowledge of struggling Otero County residents and her hands-on work to help them. It described her as a survivor of homelessness and domestic violence and a certified nursing assistant.

She founded Royal Angels, a group serving children with special needs, which the chapter said was inspired by her granddaughter. The committee said she is committed to children, families, seniors, veterans and people with mental health issues and disabilities.

Nagamine is a lifelong Alamogordo resident and a former Mrs. New Mexico pageant titleholder, according to Source NM's voter guide. She has said the district's problems, including aging water infrastructure, child welfare and housing for military families, do not belong to one party.

Block has represented the district since 2023. He and Nagamine are the only candidates listed for the seat on the Nov. 3 ballot, according to The Ballot Brief.

Statewide, the chapter endorsed Deb Haaland and Stephanie Garcia Richard for the governor's office. It credited Garcia Richard, the current land commissioner, with raising bonding requirements so oil and gas operators pay for well cleanup.

The chapter also backed Amanda López Askin for secretary of state and Attorney General Raúl Torrez for a second term. For commissioner of public lands it chose Juan de Jesus Sanchez III, citing his support for writing the Land Office's cultural resources office into state law.

Its state House endorsements include Reps. Liz Thomson and Cristina Parajon, among others.

The chapter is also urging a "yes" vote on three constitutional amendments. One, Amendment 4, would pay legislators a salary starting in 2029, set at the state median, now about $67,800.

The chapter says its mission is to "explore, enjoy and protect the planet." Its stated priorities are protecting climate, air, water, wildlife and public lands in New Mexico and West Texas.

The Rio Grande Chapter is volunteer-led and says it represents more than 10,000 members in New Mexico and West Texas. It describes candidate endorsements as part of its nonpartisan mission. The Nagamine endorsement was authorized and paid for by the chapter's political action committee.

Election Day is Nov. 3. Voter information is available at NMvote.gov.

item.title: Kite festival to fill the sky over Alamogordo labyrinth park Oct. 17
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Families can build, decorate and fly kites for free on Saturday, Oct. 17, at the Dream Higher Autumn Kite Festival. The daylong event runs from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. at Trinity Turtle Healing Labyrinth Park, 7440 U.S. Highway 54.

CAPPED Inc., a local 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded by registered nurse Tresa VanWinkle, is hosting the festival as a stress-reducing day out for all ages. Its theme is "Kites Connect Generations," and organizers are inviting grandparents, parents and children to register and fly together.

The day ends after dark with a lighted kite exhibition.

Registration and kite building open the day. The first 80 registered children ages 6 to 12 will receive a free white kite kit to decorate. The first 50 children under 6 will receive a free white pinwheel, and organizers say adults who are "still young at heart" can ask for one too.

Volunteers in the kite-building tents will supply markers and help with decorating. Families register as a group, and organizers say the contact cell number will be used only to share news of future events.

Registration, kite building and pinwheel decorating run from 10 a.m. to noon. Hot dogs with all the fixings will be served under the Big Pavilion from noon to 1 p.m., with donations appreciated. Kite flying runs from 1 to 5 p.m., followed by a dinner break from 5 to 7 p.m. The lighted kite exhibition closes the day from 7 to 9 p.m.

For safety, kite flying is limited to the park's West Kite Flying Field. Organizers suggest bringing a flashlight for the evening exhibition.

Visitors can walk the park's Head, Body and Tail labyrinths throughout the day. Organizers say the site is believed to be the largest concrete labyrinth in the world, citing its listing on the World Wide Labyrinth Locator. They encourage families to take a break, walk, breathe and connect with each other and with nature.

Four dragon kites will be raffled during the afternoon. The first ticket is free at registration, and additional tickets are two for $1. The red dragon will be drawn at noon, the blue at 1 p.m., the yellow at 2 p.m. and the purple at 3 p.m.

Additional kites and supplies will be for sale. Those include commercial kite kits, special-design kites, large kites for adults, string reels and LED string light kits. All proceeds will fund next year's events, organizers said.

VanWinkle, who also serves as executive director, founded CAPPED in Alamogordo in 2000 to meet a growing need for cancer information and support in the rural community, according to the organization's website. The group has since broadened its work to wellness and prevention more generally. In 2023 it changed the words behind its name to Center Advancing Primary Prevention thru Enlightened Decisions.

The festival fits that focus. CAPPED says VanWinkle sees addressing chronic stress as key to preventing chronic disease, and views places like the labyrinth park as essential to community health. The organization's stated vision is "a world without cancer and other preventable disease."

The festival is a community service project supported by Otero County. The park, a CAPPED community health project, was partially funded by the New Mexico Economic Development Department's Outdoor Recreation Division. It is open to walkers around the clock, year-round.

The Dream Higher Autumn Kite Festival runs from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 17, at Trinity Turtle Healing Labyrinth Park, 7440 U.S. Highway 54, Alamogordo. Admission is free. Organizers recommend hats, sunglasses, sunscreen and plenty of water, and all children must be accompanied by a responsible adult. For more information, text or call 575-430-7798.

item.title: Gary "Silver Fox" Hveem, Alamogordo's winningest football coach, dies at 86
item.description:
Alamogordo N. M. - Gary Hveem, the winningest and longest-tenured head football coach in Alamogordo High School history, died this week after battling an undisclosed illness. He was 86.

Known in Alamogordo as the "Silver Fox," Hveem spent 44 years as a teacher, coach and athletic director. He led the Tigers for ten seasons, 1976 through 1985, winning about 70 percent of his games. The Alamogordo Tiger Football Program announced his passing "with heavy hearts," remembering a coach who left a lasting mark on the players, coaches and community he served.

The road to Alamogordo

A native of Osage, Iowa, Hveem earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Northern Iowa and a master's from the University of Missouri. He first came to New Mexico in 1971 as offensive coordinator at Eastern New Mexico University, then returned home as head coach at Central High School in Waterloo, Iowa. Tom Forni, a former Eastern colleague then coaching at Carlsbad, kept him posted on New Mexico openings. When the Tiger job came open, Hveem applied.

He assembled a new staff and set about rebuilding the program, bringing a stability it had lacked for decades. He also reached out to the community, writing a weekly guest column in the Alamogordo News, "A Sporting Glance," that answered questions from parents of prospective players.

Building a contender

By 1979 his Tigers were ranked No. 1 in the state early in the season, with Bob Sepulveda, Curtis Fortney, Tom Jones and Gregg Martin on his staff. Quarterback Todd Hveem, his son, set the school's season passing record that fall. When a district vote left Alamogordo out of the playoffs after a three-way tie, Hveem publicly challenged the process and pushed for a statistical tiebreaker.

His 100th career win came in November 1980, a 41-12 victory over Las Cruces at Aggie Memorial Stadium. In 1981, a 54-8 homecoming rout of Las Cruces clinched the program's first district title in 36 years, and a 14-0 win over Santa Fe sent the Tigers to the state semifinals. In 1982 they reached the Class AAAA final, falling to Clovis 20-7.

The 1985 season

The 1985 Tigers finished 10-0 with a 32-16 win over Roswell, the first and only regular season without a loss or tie in school history. At quarterback was junior Greg Stephens, whom Sepulveda had persuaded a skeptical Hveem to try.

Alamogordo shut out Del Norte 28-0 and beat Highland 28-6 in the playoffs. The title game was Hveem's 200th as a head coach. More than 10,000 fans watched the Tigers take a 12-9 halftime lead before Clovis pulled away, 36-12. "The best team may have won today, but not the best guys," he told his players.

It was his last game on the Tiger sideline. In May 1986 the Alamogordo Daily News reported he was resigning to become an assistant director of the New Mexico Activities Association, chosen over some 60 other applicants. "Tiger football is not dependent on any one person," he said on his way out.

Administrator in two states

Hveem later returned to Iowa, where his work at Iowa City High School earned him Athletic Director of the Year honors in 1995. In 1996 he became the first athletic director of Rio Rancho Public Schools, building a program from scratch in a district that had been K-8. By his retirement in 2007, Rio Rancho High had won state titles in six sports. He was inducted into the district's Hall of Honor in 2023, and the school's press box bears his name. Longtime Rams volleyball coach Toby Manzanares called him "the visionary architect of the school's athletic program."

Honored at home

Alamogordo did not forget him. The Otero County Commission proclaimed September 4, 2021, "Coach Gary Hveem Day." That evening, a celebration at Roadrunner Emporium on New York Avenue hosted by journalist and sports historian, Chris Edwards, honored Hveem and Sepulveda as the school's winningest football and track and field coaches. It also launched a book available on Amazon, Coach Bob Sepulveda: The Hveem Years, written by Chris Edwards and Rene Sepulveda.

The two coaches remained close friends for life and spoke often, up until recent weeks. Sepulveda remembered Hveem as one of the greatest coaches he knew and one of the dearest friends he and his late wife, Marilyn, ever had. He said Hveem's commitment to student achievement will be remembered for generations.

Hveem is survived by Fran, his wife of 65 years, whom he met in kindergarten, and four children: Todd, Stephanie, Jennifer and Joshua. Funeral services are pending. He will be laid to rest in his hometown of Osage.

item.title: Race Day in Ruidoso: The XTERRA World Championship Comes Home
item.description:
RUIDOSO, N.M. — The XTERRA World Championship returns to American soil this morning, when the elite field dives into Grindstone Lake at 9:15 a.m. for the sport’s 30th-anniversary title race. By early afternoon, new world champions will have been crowned in Wingfield Park, in the middle of a village that has spent more than a year getting ready for this weekend.

Thirty years, and a homecoming

XTERRA began on Maui in 1996 and crowned its world champions there for 25 years. In 2022 the race moved to Molveno, Italy, for four editions beneath the Brenta Dolomites. Today it lands in Ruidoso, a mountain village of ponderosa pine and switchbacks at about 6,900 feet in southern New Mexico.

The village is not a one-year stop. Ruidoso has committed to host the championship through 2028.

“This opportunity is a full-circle moment to bring the XTERRA World Championship back to the USA, marking a 30-year legacy of exploration and adventure,” Steve Andrus, XTERRA’s Americas tour manager, said when the deal was announced.

Athletes from more than 45 countries are in town, and the elite field races for a $100,000 purse. The men’s race is expected to include three-time world champion Arthur Serrières of France and Sullivan Middaugh, the 22-year-old American whose father, Josiah, won the title in 2015.

Mayor Sharon McDonald of Alamogordo joined the host mayor of the Village of Ruidoso: Lynn D. Crawford and the nearby City of Ruidoso Downs: Carroll Scott in viewing the event and welcoming the world to the region.

Ruidoso Mayor Crawford said this was a huge opportunity for businesses, residents to collaborate and the region to be seen by participants around the world as a place to want to visit, vacation and celebrate. He also mentioned the air service direct from Denver into the Ruidoso airport was bringing in teams and visitors adding another service and regional enhancement to ease of travel. 

Alamogordo Mayor Sharon McDonald mentioned the joy of meeting athletes from France, Italy, Japan and around the world as well as US athletes from all over our country. She said several had mentioned, “coming down to White Sands National Park and visiting  Alamogordo’s restaurants and shops  thus the games have a regional significance and economic impact.”


The course

The full-distance race covers 38.5 kilometers. It starts at Grindstone Lake and finishes downhill into Wingfield Park. Altitude is the constant: the lake sits near 7,000 feet, and the bike course climbs toward 7,800.

The day opens with a 1.5-kilometer swim, two loops of Grindstone Lake. The water measured 63 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit on this same weekend a year ago.

From there, athletes ride a 27-kilometer mountain bike course with nearly 2,950 feet of climbing. It runs up to Grindstone Mesa on tight, rocky singletrack, with loose surfaces and switchbacks, before a fast descent to transition. Early announcements listed a 30-kilometer bike leg; the final course is 27.

The race ends with a 10-kilometer trail run. The first three-quarters is singletrack through the pines. The rest crosses a disc golf course and neighborhood streets before dropping into Wingfield Park and the finish line.

“If there was ever a mountain town built for an XTERRA event, Ruidoso is it,” age-group athlete Michael Pearce said in a Slowtwitch preview of the race.

The weekend from here


Three world championship races remain: the full distance today and two youth races Sunday. All times are Mountain Daylight Time.

Today’s elite start at 9:15 a.m. is followed by the age-group start at 9:45, both at Grindstone Lake. The first finisher is expected at Wingfield Park around 11:30 a.m., and the bike course closes at 2:30 p.m. The full-distance awards ceremony runs from 7 to 10 p.m. at the Ruidoso Convention Center, with the XTERRA after party to follow.

Sunday belongs to the next generation. The Youth A world championship, for athletes ages 14 and 15, starts at 10 a.m. over a super sprint course: a 400-meter swim, a 7-kilometer bike and a 2-kilometer run. At 11:30 a.m., Youth B and Junior athletes, ages 16 through 19, race a 750-meter swim, a 15-kilometer bike and a 5-kilometer run. An open sprint for anyone 16 and older starts at the same time.

Open sprint awards are set for 2 p.m. Sunday at Wingfield Park. The weekend closes with the youth awards and closing ceremony from 5 to 8 p.m. at the convention center. That ceremony is open to the community with a dinner ticket, sold at the XTERRA Expo in Wingfield Park.

How to watch

Spectators should park in Midtown and ride the shuttle, because the Grindstone Lake lot is reserved for athletes on both race days. Public parking is available along Midtown streets and at the northwest corner of Wingfield Park.

Two shuttles run a continuous loop from 7 a.m. to 4 p.m. between Wingfield Park, Grindstone Lake and the athlete lot; look for the yellow XTERRA flags. The athlete-lot stop closes from about 9 a.m. to 2 p.m., and bikes are not allowed on board. The Village of Ruidoso has posted road closures for the weekend, so check them before driving between venues.

The finish line is the place to be. The expo in Wingfield Park runs from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. today, and the Family Zone is open from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.

From anywhere else, all three championship races stream live on XTERRA’s YouTube channel. Coverage starts at 9 a.m. today, and at 9:50 and 11:20 a.m. Sunday.

Dress in layers. October days in Ruidoso average about 63 degrees, with cool mornings at the lake.

A village on the world stage

For Ruidoso, the weekend is a marker of recovery as much as a race. The community has been rebuilding since the fires and floods of 2024, and its visitor center still operates from a bank on Sudderth Drive because of flood damage.

The village earned the championship in steps. It staged its first XTERRA race in August 2025 as a test, then hosted the inaugural IRONMAN 70.3 Ruidoso in July 2026.

“We’re ready for the world stage as a premier destination for outdoor adventure sports as we welcome outdoor enthusiasts from around the globe to experience our trails, our hospitality, and the unique spirit of Ruidoso,” Mayor Lynn Crawford said in announcing the host agreement.

Race week has reached well past the course. Athletes have been in town for over a week. Events began on Thursday. Free yoga sessions, guided hikes on Moon Mountain and Grindstone Mesa, line dancing at Win, Place & Show and a Thursday welcome concert by the Phil Hamilton Band were open to residents and visitors alongside the athletes. Registered athletes also carry a digital Shop Hop pass for discounts at Midtown businesses through Sunday.

The world comes back in 2027 and 2028. For Ruidoso and the region, today is the first of three chances to show it belongs on the calendar.

item.title: In Memory of J Kelly Clayton Carnes
item.description:
J Kelly Clayton Carnes was born January 9, 1970, in Denver, CO, to Marvin and Connie Carnes of Lone Wolf, OK. Raised on the family farm in Oklahoma, Kelly developed early the love of animals, open spaces, and the natural world that remained an important part of him throughout his life.

Kelly began helping his father on the farm at a young age and graduated from Lone Wolf High School in 1988. He earned a bachelor's degree in Agricultural Science from Cameron University in Lawton, OK, before earning his master's degree in Orientation and Mobility from Texas Tech University in Lubbock, TX.

After completing his certification, Kelly went to work for the New Mexico School for the Blind and Visually Impaired in Alamogordo, NM. For more than 30 years, he devoted his career to working with children with visual impairments, helping them develop the skills and confidence to move through the world with greater independence. His work brought together qualities that were distinctly Kelly: independence, practicality, patience, and a preference for doing rather than making a fuss about doing.

Kelly married Terri Payne in 1995 and helped raise her three sons, Chad, Brad, and Daniel. He married Tiffany Randall in 2016.

Kelly loved God, his family and friends, animals, and the outdoors. He was happiest close to nature-feeling cool grass or hot concrete beneath his bare feet, holding the animals at Runyan Ranch, or simply spending time outside. Restless by nature, Kelly was rarely one to sit still for long.

He was also an avid and curious reader with interests that ranged from historical texts and the Bible to health and natural approaches to wellness. Kelly had his own way of looking at the world and was never particularly concerned with fitting neatly into anyone else's categories. Those who knew him well knew his distinctive sense of humor, his independent streak, and the contradictions that made him unmistakably unique.

Kelly valued his relationships deeply, even if sentiment and ceremony were not always his style. He was, in fact, much more comfortable slipping quietly away than standing around for a long goodbye. But the friendships he built over the years endured, and the people fortunate enough to become part of his circle knew the loyalty and affection beneath that independent exterior.

Kelly is survived by his mother, Connie; his sister, Marla; his dear friends Rick, Jami, Loana, Mary, Jeremiah, and many others. We would like to thank Inhabit Hospice Care for helping us navigate this difficult time.

Kelly will be laid to rest in Ruidoso, NM. A service is planned for a later date.

item.title: In Memory of John H Russell
item.description:
John H Russell, age 78, passed away peacefully at home in Ruidoso, New Mexico, on September 21, 2026.

Born on February 1, 1948, in Raton, New Mexico, John H Russell served honorably in the United States Coast Guard from 1966 to 1970. After his military service, he remained an active presence in the Ruidoso community, giving his time to organizations including the Homebuilders Association and the Veterans of New Mexico.

John was known throughout town as a familiar and friendly face. He was a regular at Club Gas, where he spent many happy hours visiting with local friends, discussing history, exchanging stories, and sharing opinions on a wide range of topics. He was remarkably intelligent and found great enjoyment in conversation and the lively exchange of ideas.

He was preceded in death by his parents, Oliver Marion Russell and Alma Margaline Owen, and by his brothers, Owen M. Russell and R. Randy Russell.

John is survived by his wife, Durene (Hein) Russell; his children, Mark Russell and JoLynn Russell, both of Ruidoso, Eric Russell of Jacksonville, Florida, and Jeff Russell of Alamogordo, New Mexico; and his grandsons, Deric, Tyler, and Hayden. He is also survived by a niece and grandnephew of Ruidoso, a nephew of Huntsville, Alabama, a grandnephew of Folsom, New Mexico, and a nephew of Whitefish, Montana.

A committal ceremony with military honors will be held on Friday, October 23, 2026, at Fort Stanton State Veterans Cemetery, 1398 Hwy 220, Fort Stanton, New Mexico. A Celebration of Life will follow at 2:00 PM on Sunday, October 25, 2026, at Calvary Chapel Ruidoso, 707 Mechem Dr, Ruidoso, New Mexico.

In lieu of flowers, donations may be made in John's honor to US Veterans of New Mexico, PO Box 356, Alto, NM 88312. He will be remembered by those who knew him for his conversation, his wit, and his lasting presence in the community.

item.title: Organ Mountain sweeps Lady Tigers in straight Volleyball sets
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Organ Mountain swept the Alamogordo Lady Tigers on Saturday, winning a district volleyball match in straight sets, 25-14, 25-20, 25-19.

The loss on Alamogordo's home floor drops the Lady Tigers to 6-10 overall and 0-2 in district play.

Alamogordo's best stretch came early in the second set, when the Lady Tigers built a five-point lead. Organ Mountain erased it and closed out the set.

Organ Mountain controlled the opening set from the start. The Knights led 10-5, stretched the margin to 16-9 and finished off a 25-14 win.

Alamogordo answered in the second set, jumping out to a 7-2 lead. Organ Mountain chipped away and moved in front 11-10, then held narrow leads of 15-13 and 21-18 before taking the set 25-20 for a 2-0 advantage.

The Knights opened the third set with a 13-7 lead. The Lady Tigers rallied to pull within three at 17-14, but Organ Mountain held them off and closed out the sweep, 25-19.

The Lady Tigers stay in district play with a road trip to Las Cruces. Alamogordo plays at Mayfield on Tuesday, still looking for its first district win of the season.

item.title: XTERRA Worlds 30: Middaugh gives home crowd a world title in Ruidoso
item.description:
RUIDOSO NM  — The world came up the mountain this weekend, and an American sent the home crowd home happy.

Sullivan Middaugh ran away with the elite men's race at the 2026 XTERRA World Championship on Saturday, giving the home crowd its first title in 11 years. France's Alizée Patiès won the elite women's race. Both are first-time world champions.

The off-road triathlon's 30th anniversary brought athletes and supporters from 41 countries to Lincoln County. Ruidoso is the third home of the championship, after Maui, Hawaii, and Molveno, Italy.

Full-distance racers swam 1.5 kilometers in Grindstone Lake, a little under a mile. They then rode 27 kilometers, about 17 miles, of rocky singletrack around Grindstone Mesa and ran 10 kilometers, or 6.2 miles, through village streets and forest trails.

The mountain morning was cold. An hour before the start, the lake measured about 65 degrees and the air about 53.

Middaugh won going away, but his day nearly came apart in the first minutes of the bike leg. Gálvez led the field out of Grindstone Lake in 18:21, with Middaugh and his younger brother Porter close behind. Then both leaders went down. Gálvez crashed on the first corner and Middaugh on the third, losing his bike computer.

With no power numbers to look at, Middaugh rode by feel.

"I think it was maybe a blessing in disguise not to have power data," he said.

It worked. His 1:07:18 bike split was the fastest in the men's field, and his 39:00 run was the fastest too. He said he trusted his uphill running at altitude, pushed every climb and let the descents roll.

Gálvez picked himself up and held on to second, a finish few race predictions had him making. Nielsen, a crowd favorite, started the bike in 13th and worked his way up to bronze. It is his fourth straight World Championship podium.

France's Arthur Serrières finished fourth and countryman Maxim Chané fifth.

The winner was not the only Middaugh near the front. Sullivan's father, former XTERRA world champion Josiah Middaugh, finished sixth. Younger brother Porter crossed the line seventh despite a hard crash on the bike. That put three members of one family in the world's top seven.

"Just a proud day," Josiah Middaugh said.

Sullivan said the win meant everything to him. He and his brother grew up going to their father's races.

Patiès won the elite women's race in 2:36:19, finishing 6 minutes 14 seconds ahead of Italy's Marta Menditto. Australia's Maeve Kennedy took bronze.

Costa Rica's Raquel Solis and France's Emma Ducreux came out of the water together in 20:38. Patiès said the swim was a struggle, so she let the lead group go and settled into her own pace. She started the bike in third.

She did not stay there long. Patiès had the lead by the first bike checkpoint, and her 1:20:45 split was the fastest of the women's race. The gap held up through a run she said hurt everywhere, especially on the second lap.

"It's a lifelong dream," Patiès said.

Menditto ran her way to silver with the fastest women's run split, 50:42, passing Ducreux on the second lap. Kennedy also got past Ducreux late on that lap to reach the podium. She credited her family, training partners and community for getting her there

The village made an impression on its guests. Australia's Hannah-Lee Young, sixth in the elite women's race, said Ruidoso's small-town feel reminds her of where she grew up.

"I walk down the street now and everyone says hello," Young said.

In the age-group championships, France's Simon Gourgues and Inès de Sousa posted the fastest overall men's and women's times. Both won their 20–24 divisions. New Zealand's Arna Craig took second in the women's 40–44 division behind New Caledonia's Caroline Favier, who passed her on the second run lap.

Racing wraps up Sunday, Oct. 11, with two shorter triathlons and the closing ceremony.

item.title: Alamogordo police log: Drug task force arrests, five-car pileup and four DWI arrests mark week
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Alamogordo police reported drug trafficking arrests, a five-vehicle crash, and a string of weekend DWI arrests in the department's weekly activity log for Sept. 28 through Oct. 4.

The week opened Monday with officers assisting the White Mountain Drug Task Force. Two people were arrested on charges of trafficking a controlled substance and conspiracy, and a third, already in custody, was served with a criminal complaint for possession of a controlled substance. A fourth person was arrested Friday on a possession warrant during another task force assist.

Also Monday, a man was arrested on a charge of aggravated battery against a household member causing great bodily harm following a domestic violence investigation. Another man, arrested on a warrant and charged with resisting an officer, was later served with a complaint for aggravated stalking.

On Tuesday, police, fire and ambulance crews responded to a five-car pileup at the south U.S. 54/70 junction. Officers said a silver pickup failed to brake in time. Everyone reporting injuries was treated and released at the scene, and the pickup's driver received several traffic citations.

The same day, a disturbance at the Otero Village Apartments led to citations for three people, and a man was arrested at his residence on charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon and negligent use of a deadly weapon.

On Wednesday, officers responding to an alarm at Dollar Boots and Jean found the front windows damaged. Police said a man entered the business, walked around and left. Video and photos were recovered, and the investigation continues.

Three people faced cruelty to children allegations during the week: two were cited Friday after a disturbance, and a man was arrested Sunday on charges of assault and cruelty to children after a disturbance in the 1100 block of Dewey Avenue.

Four people were arrested on DWI charges, one Saturday and three Sunday. One of the Sunday drivers was released to a military supervisor.

Three juveniles, ages 13 and 14, were referred to juvenile probation on allegations including battery, disorderly conduct and battery against a household member.

Officers also responded to five unattended deaths. Four appeared to be from natural causes. The fifth, involving a 59-year-old found unresponsive Thursday, remains under investigation.

Other entries included warrant arrests, trespassing, shoplifting, and citations for cruelty to animals and malicious use of a telephone.

The log lists major activity only, not every call for service. All charges are allegations, and those accused are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.
